name: ocaml
desc: General purpose programming language in the ML family
why: A mainstream-ish ML language with a real compiler, though it is widely known and only a close call here.

brief.what_it_is: OCaml is a general-purpose programming language in the ML family, described on its homepage as an industrial-strength functional programming language with an emphasis on expressiveness and safety. It takes source files or interactive input and produces output through two compilers: a bytecode compiler that the homepage says generates small, highly portable executables, and a native-code compiler that produces efficient machine code. The homepage shows an interactive top-level session, where typed expressions such as a square function and a recursive factorial return values with their inferred types. The toolchain also includes the opam package manager, the utop REPL, and the odoc documentation generator.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches OCaml as a language whose lightweight but expressive type system catches more bugs at compile time, while garbage collection lets developers focus on application logic instead of memory management. It cites large, complex codebases that stay easy to maintain and refactor.
brief.how_it_works: Code is compiled either to bytecode or to native machine code, and a garbage collector handles memory. Packages are installed through opam, which the install page says installs both the compiler and additional packages into isolated environments called switches. The homepage says the type system infers types, as the top-level session shows the inferred signature val square : int -> int.

commands_seen.context: Homepage top-level example: defines a square function, which the REPL echoes back with the inferred type int -> int.
Homepage top-level example: calling the square function, which returns 9.
Homepage top-level example: start of a recursive factorial definition spanning two lines (if x <= 1 then 1 else x * factorial (x - 1)).
Homepage top-level example: evaluates factorial on 5, returning 120.
Install page: run this in the shell if you declined the opam init prompt to add the current switch's tools to PATH.

brief.install_notes: On Linux, macOS, or *BSD the install page says to first ensure gcc, build-essential, curl, unzip, and bubblewrap are installed, then install opam with a script from its GitHub repository (the exact curl line was not captured in the fetched text). Next run opam init, which creates a default switch and asks whether to add a shell hook for PATH. Then install the OCaml Platform Tools, including the Dune build system, into the current switch with a command not captured in the fetched text. On Windows, opam has supported Windows natively since 2.2.0 and is the recommended route; the steps are run in PowerShell or Command Prompt, opam init asks about Unix support infrastructure (option 1 lets opam manage it), and the switch is activated with a cmd or PowerShell command. The page says opam initialisation may take several minutes on Windows. Distro package managers may ship an older opam that does not support the latest compiler.
brief.standout: Unlike many ML-family languages, OCaml ships a real native compiler alongside a bytecode one, and its homepage leans on a published industrial case study (a XenServer product group) to back its reliability claims. The opam switch model, with isolated per-project compiler and package environments, is a notable part of the workflow. The scout note calls it widely known and only a close call for this catalogue.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists latest release 5.5.1 dated 2026-09-05, described as bug fixes for 5.5.0 with security hardening of the Marshal module, plus a Long Term Support release 4.14.4. The release feed also shows opam 2.6.1 dated 07 Oct 2026 and opam 2.6.0 dated 16 Sep 2026. The homepage has recent dated changelog entries.
brief.caveats: The homepage is largely marketing copy and the fetched text dropped the code blocks on the install page, so the exact install commands for opam and Dune were not captured. The install instructions depend on opam, and Linux users need several system packages first. Windows setup uses a different path from Linux and macOS. The homepage makes qualitative claims about reliability and performance without benchmarks. No license information was seen on the pages fetched.
quotes: An industrial-strength functional programming language with an emphasis on expressiveness and safety
OCaml's package manager, opam, installs both the compiler, as well as any additional packages.
The bytecode compiler generates small, highly portable executables blazingly fast; the native code compiler produces highly-efficient machine code.
